title: Unsupervised machine learning reveals previously missed hydraulic-fracturing seismicity in Live Oak County
summary: An unsupervised repeating-signal detector, combined with template matching, exposed small earthquake bursts in a region of the Eagle Ford shale where conventional catalogs had detected little seismicity. The authors report that the new events temporally coincided with hydraulic-fracturing activity, and their regional analysis found detectable seismicity began after injection flux exceeded about two million barrels per month despite similar cumulative injection volume; this supports, but does not prove, a causal role for injection rate and is limited by sparse station coverage.
ai_technology: Repeating Signal Detector (RSD), an unsupervised machine-learning waveform-family detector

evidence.tested: An unsupervised repeating-signal detector, combined with template matching, exposed small earthquake bursts in a region of the Eagle Ford shale where conventional catalogs had detected little seismicity.
evidence.unknown: The RSD detections were manually inspected and some event locations were poorly constrained; the authors note station density limits detection and do not establish causation from temporal correlation alone. This paper extends an earlier Eagle Ford study but reports a distinct Live Oak County seismicity region and subsequent time-period catalog.
evidence.ai_role: RSD searched continuous seismograms without relying on preselected earthquake templates, clustered similar signals, and revealed small-magnitude event bursts missed by the previous catalog. Researchers manually inspected signals and analyzed their timing relative to hydraulic-fracturing records.
